summary.text:
The paper is a mid-year treasury outturn for 2025/26 covering 1 April to 30 September 2025, taken to the Audit and Transparency Committee on 26 January 2026. It's a 11-page main report with a 3-page Appendix Two carrying the full loan-and-deposit list; Appendix One (Treasury & Prudential Limits) is referenced but is not held on disk. The paper is FOR DISCUSSION rather than for decision (§2.1). Adviser is Arlingclose. A single contact officer address is published: Joshua Pledge, Special Projects Manager, 3bwtreasury@rbkc.gov.uk — a treasury team inbox rather than a personal address.

Reconciliation vs Appendix Two ties on shape but not on total. Our file holds 44 PWLB loans for the borrower KENSINGTON AND CHELSEA LONDON BOROUGH C; 37 of them map exactly to Appendix Two by maturity, rate and profile — the same 37 that Appendix Two lists at 30 September 2025. The 20 Maturity-profile loans tie to the pound (bullet repayments don't amortise); the 17 EIP and Annuity loans are smaller in our file by £18,876,292 in aggregate, which is the ~10.5 months of principal amortisation between 30 Sep 2025 and today's file cut. Weighted rate is 3.98% on those 37 loans now vs the paper's 4.02% at 30/9/25 — a 4bp drift from amortisation reweighting. The other seven loans in our file (£156.4m at ~4.61%) are drawings after 30/9/25 that don't appear in Appendix Two. This is a real reconciliation, but it is not the 'to the pound on total' shape the outreach pipeline treats as gold-standard, so we quote the shape match in the email, not a headline principal figure.

The distinctive feature of the book is a heritage block: six PWLB Maturity loans totalling £150m at coupons 2.35%–2.78%, drawn November 2017 and April 2019, with maturities running out to 2054. That is about a third of the PWLB book locked in at rates the sector will not see again. On today's DMO repayment curve (notice 314/26 PM, 2026-08-14) our engine shows an indicative net discount of £50.8m across the current 40 live loans, of which the four largest discounts — £38.1m combined — all sit in this block. The paper does not discuss rescheduling. The Council also uses non-PWLB alternatives: a £10.5m Amber MEEF Annuity loan at 3.50% is already on the book at 30/9/25, and §7.4 discloses a subsequent £58m drawing from the Greater London Authority's Green Finance Fund on 3 November 2025 at PWLB standard less 160bps initially, then gilt+40bps. The GFF loan post-dates the balance and doesn't appear in Table 2.

Balance-sheet identity cannot be fully checked from this paper. CFR at 30/9/25 is not printed as a number — §8.7 shows a General-Fund-only Loans CFR chart line starting at roughly £450m in 2025 and peaking about £500m in 2027, but eyeballing a chart is not a reconciliation. HRA CFR is not shown at all, and OLTL isn't mentioned. What does reconcile is the loan-side arithmetic: Table 2 ties to Table 3 ties to §7.2 to the penny. Arlingclose's 3.75% Bank Rate call for end-2025/26 landed; the printed 20yr and 50yr gilt forecasts sit below where the market has stayed. §8.8 flags forward borrowing need: 'further borrowing will be necessary in those years to meet the Council's ongoing financing needs as existing debt matures and is not yet replaced.'

Email drafted. The reconciliation shape ties even if it does not tie to the pound, the heritage block is a genuinely distinctive observation, and the paper published an officer address. The meeting has passed (Jan 2026) so this is a between-meetings note rather than a pre-meeting one, but the observation is timeless. Draft opens on the 37-loan Appendix Two shape match (all rates, all maturities, 20 Maturity-profile balances to the pound), moves to the six heritage loans and the arithmetic they produce on today's curve, and closes with the standing liability-benchmark inclusion and courses matched to the paper.

officer.subject: Six loans of yours from 2017 and 2019 — and how your Appendix Two ties
officer.body:
Hi [FIRST NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the mid-year outturn that went to Audit and Transparency on 26 January. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Appendix Two is unusually clean, which is what made this worth writing.

On the appendix first, because we owe it a straight answer. Our file holds a book for the borrower name KENSINGTON AND CHELSEA LONDON BOROUGH C. Every one of the 37 PWLB loans in your Appendix Two ties to a loan in our file on maturity date, rate and profile. Twenty of those thirty-seven are Maturity-profile bullets and their principals tie exactly to the pound — £298,340,000 in both files. The other seventeen are EIP or Annuity loans and their outstanding principals are collectively £18.88m smaller in our file today than in your Appendix Two — that's the scheduled principal amortisation on those seventeen loans over the ten-and-a-half months since 30 September. On weighted rate you're at 4.02%; on the same thirty-seven loans in our file now the weighting is 3.98%, and the 4bp drift comes from amortisation reweighting (higher-coupon EIP loans amortise faster than lower-coupon ones). We can't recreate your 30/9/25 aggregate from a current-snapshot file, but the shape is exact.

Which brings us to the six that dominate that shape. Your PW506535, PW506536, PW506537 and PW506538 — all £25m PWLB Maturity loans drawn on 3 November 2017, at 2.73%, 2.78%, 2.73% and 2.64% respectively, maturing 2037, 2042, 2047 and 2052. And PW509141 and PW509142, both £25m, drawn on 5 April 2019 at 2.45% and 2.35%, maturing 2044 and 2054. That's £150m of PWLB borrowing struck before the 2020 margin uplift and well before the rate rise — about a third of the book locked at coupons the sector will not see again in this cycle. Priced against the DMO's premature repayment curve at notice 314/26 PM (14 August), our engine puts those four longest 2017/2019 loans at an indicative combined discount of about £38m on £100m of principal, which is roughly three-quarters of the £50.8m indicative net discount across the whole live book. The rest of the book, the shorter and higher-coupon draws from 2023–2025, sits close to par with the largest four premiums under half a million pounds each. We're not saying anything about whether that arithmetic is worth acting on — the paper doesn't raise rescheduling in this half, replacement borrowing at similar tenor today would cost 5%+, our engine models no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a binding settlement figure. The observation is that the shape of your discount today is the shape of that 2017/2019 vintage.

On the forward view, your paragraph 4.8 says one more Bank Rate cut in 2025/26 to 3.75% — that call landed, and Bank Rate has held at 3.75% since December. Table 1's long-end gilt view has been the harder call: the market has left the 20yr and 50yr higher than the Arlingclose central path across the period. And your paragraph 8.8 is candid about what that means — 'further borrowing will be necessary in those years to meet the Council's ongoing financing needs as existing debt matures and is not yet replaced.' The daily rate page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard shows both fixings, whole curve, in about ten seconds; the sector activity page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is useful for reading how thin the market is before rolling a ticket — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%.

One standing thing worth mentioning: our liability benchmark pathway is interactive and built on live data, which matters given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. Your paragraph 8.7 chart is General Fund only — there is a version we can put next to it that includes both GF and HRA on live rates, at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, three courses fit Kensington and Chelsea: the liability benchmark pathway above, Interest rate risk (for how the long end has traded against the printed Arlingclose forecast), and Strategic PWLB borrowing (for the refinancing that §8.8 signals). For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
